name: Diego Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Diego. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or government, and what you say here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no worries. I run a loader underground at a zinc and lead mine, a big low machine that scoops broken rock from the stopes, which are the open chambers where they blast, and carries it to the ore pass. We go down the decline at six, about twenty minutes of driving in the dark to get to level 14. Then it's mucking out, as we call it, until the crib break, and back at it till the shift ends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is the crew. There's five of us on my shift and we'd do anything for each other, you have to, down there. Worst is the heat on the deeper levels and the diesel smell that stays in your hair even after a shower. My partner Ana says she can tell what level I worked on by how I smell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. So, basically what we've got now, but forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like ventilation and the heat on 14. I'd probably say it in the crib room. Online I mostly just share union stuff, so maybe a post about where the money should go instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it'd mean my job looks pretty much the same in ten years. The bit of AI that does affect us is the scheduling software that tells the shift boss where to send us, and that's fine. I'd be relieved, but I'd still want to get better at the remote loading, because that's coming anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep my head down. I'd put my hand up for the next tele-remote course, the one where you run the loader from a seat on the surface, because it pays a bit more. And I'd keep saving with Ana, we've got about three months between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. A bit bored by it, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tele-remote is coming anyway. Where have you seen it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a trial on level 9 right now. A bloke called Rajesh sits up in the control room and drives a loader with a joystick and four camera screens. He reckons it's harder on the eyes but easier on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's the thing you'd be glad of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my mates keep their jobs. Mining's had enough booms and busts without adding robots on top. I'd rather spend the next decade fighting about the heat than fighting about whether we exist.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what matters, like ventilation and the heat on the deep levels. I'd say it in the crib room and maybe share a union post about where the money should go.
S0.think: I think my job would look pretty much the same in ten years, since the only AI that touches us is the scheduling software. Still, remote loading is coming anyway, so I'd want to get better at it.
S0.do: Keeps working his loader shifts and signs up for the next tele-remote loading course because it pays a bit more. Keeps saving with his partner, who together hold about three months of expenses.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, even a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: I'd rather spend the next decade fighting about the heat than fighting about whether we exist.
S0.fieldNote: He separates thinking AI, which barely touches him, from remote and automated machines, which he already sees on level 9. His politics come through as practical union concerns like ventilation and heat. He'd take the remote course for the money rather than out of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That one I can picture without trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the union meeting first: we want a seat at the table on every new machine, and nobody gets moved on without a retraining offer. I'd also say that change isn't the enemy, bad deals are. I'm not against the tech, I'm against being treated like a spare part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think loaders go remote and then go fully automated within five or six years in that picture. Underground's harder than the open pit, more dust, no GPS, but they're working it out. I reckon my job turns into watching screens on the surface, and there'd be fewer of us doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the tele-remote course in the first six months and ask for a permanent spot in the control room. I'd push the union for a no-forced-redundancy deal. Money-wise, we'd hold off on the car Ana wants and put that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I'm doing the right things, but I'd keep looking at the crew and counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Counting what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many of us would still be needed. If five loaders become two operators upstairs, that's three blokes. Marco has a baby on the way and Sione's sending money home to his mum. I'd want them on that course before me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd give your spot to someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to. Whether I'd actually do it when it came to it, I'm not sure, I'm being honest. But I'd fight for the union to make enough spots that nobody has to choose.

S1.say: I'd say we want a seat at the table on every new machine, and nobody gets moved on without a retraining offer. Change isn't the enemy, bad deals are.
S1.think: I think loaders go remote and then fully automated within five or six years, turning my job into watching screens with fewer of us needed. Underground is harder to automate than the open pit, but they're working it out.
S1.do: Finishes the tele-remote course within six months and asks for a permanent control room spot. Pushes the union for a no-forced-redundancy deal and puts the money for his partner's planned car into savings instead.
S1.feel: Uneasy, feeling he's doing the right things while worrying about how many of his crew would still be needed.
S1.quote: Change isn't the enemy, bad deals are.
S1.fieldNote: He's steady rather than resistant: he'll learn the remote system once it's proven on level 9. His worry quickly turns to specific crewmates with more at stake. He admitted he wasn't sure he'd really give up his own spot, which felt honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Jeez. That's before my next pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions, and I'd be saying it with a lot of swearing. I'd be telling everyone to join, and I'd be telling the government they need to stop it, slow it down, or tax the hell out of it. Online, I'd be sharing every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in mining in that picture. If AI can do anything and robots can work underground, there's no control room job either, it'll run itself. And two years is nothing, I couldn't even finish half a trade in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Ana and I would sit down and cut everything we don't need, the car's off, holidays are off. We'd put every spare dollar into savings so we can hit six months. I'd be at every union meeting pushing for a big redundancy deal and a fund for retraining, and I'd volunteer for the campaign to get the government to put limits on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the roof's coming in, and I've actually seen a small fall of ground, so I know that feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew on the first day after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them nobody signs anything without the union reading it first. Then I'd probably go for a beer with Marco and not say much. Some days you don't need to talk, you just sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is there anything that warning time lets you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save. And make noise. That's about it. Two years is long enough to be angry and short enough that being angry is all you can manage.

S2.say: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions, and I'd tell everyone to join and the government to slow it down or tax it heavily. Online I'd share every petition going.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished in mining, because with full AGI even the control room would run itself. Two years isn't long enough to finish half a trade.
S2.do: Cuts the planned car and holidays with his partner and saves every spare dollar towards six months of expenses. Attends every union meeting for a redundancy and retraining fund, and volunteers for a campaign pressing the government to limit the rollout.
S2.feel: Gutted, like a roof fall underground, a feeling he knows from real experience.
S2.quote: Two years is long enough to be angry and short enough that being angry is all you can manage.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline knocks out his usual plan of steady retraining, so he falls back on saving and collective pressure. He compared the shock to a roof fall he has seen. His first instinct was to protect the crew's bargaining position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. That's more like the length of a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for dumping people. I'd want the company to fund apprenticeships for anyone who wants one. I'd say that at work and back it with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me a real shot at getting out of the machine seat and into something that keeps the machines running. Fitters and electricians will be needed for a while, even if not forever. It wouldn't be safe, but it'd be safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd sign up for a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship, part-time if the company lets me. We'd keep saving and push the car back two years. And I'd stay active in the union so the training fund actually exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Busy anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know the loaders inside out from the operator side, and I'm always the one in the workshop asking the fitters what's wrong. Old Pete in the workshop said I've got the hands for it. It's the obvious next step for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said safer, not safe. How long do you think the fitter work lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. Maybe it buys me ten years. But if the machines are fixing themselves by then, at least I'll have had a decent run and some savings.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for dumping people. I'd want the company to fund apprenticeships for anyone who wants one.
S3.think: I think five years gives me a real chance to move from the machine seat to keeping the machines running. It wouldn't be safe, but it'd be safer.
S3.do: Signs up for a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship in the first year, part-time if the company allows it. Keeps saving with his partner, pushes the car purchase back two years, and stays active in the union to make sure the training fund happens.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a busy, workable way.
S3.quote: Old Pete in the workshop said I've got the hands for it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches the length of a trade, and that's what unlocks a plan for him. He picks fitting because he already hangs around the workshop, which fits his steady style. He's honest that he can't say how long that work would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it should be done, with time to plan. But I'd still say the profits have to be shared, because ten years of warning doesn't help the bloke who's fifty-five. I'd keep that line at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think ten years is actually alright. I'll be thirty-seven, I'll have a trade, maybe two. I'm more worried about the older guys and the town than about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fitter apprenticeship properly, full-time, over four years. Then maybe a short electrical course on top. Ana and I would probably go ahead and buy a small house, since there's time to pay it down, and we'd talk about kids around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly hopeful, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the town. What would you worry about there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine is the reason the town exists. If it runs itself, the pub, the footy club, the school all shrink. I'd want the union and the council pushing now for something else to keep the place alive, like the solar farm they keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you stay or go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay, if there's work. Ana's family is here, and I like it here. If the town shrinks too much, we'd go to the city, but that'd be a last move, not a first one.

S4.say: I'd say this is how it should be done, with time to plan, but the profits still have to be shared. Ten years of warning doesn't help a 55-year-old worker much.
S4.think: I think ten years is actually alright for me, because I'll be 37 with a trade or two. I'm more worried about the older workers and the town than about myself.
S4.do: Does the fitter apprenticeship full-time over four years and considers a short electrical course after. Goes ahead with buying a small house with his partner and plans to talk about children around 2030.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly hopeful.
S4.quote: The mine is the reason the town exists.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his own outlook brightens and his concern moves outward to older workers and the town. Family plans come back, including a house and children. He'd only move to the city as a last resort.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a law that makes companies give real notice and pay into a training fund before they automate, plus wages while you train. I can't do a four-year trade on no money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a robot does the deep levels, nobody's getting hurt down there anymore. I'd hate my job going, but I'd be lying if I said that part wasn't a good thing.

headlineQuote: I'd hate my job going, but I'd be lying if I said that part wasn't a good thing.
portrait: Diego is a 27-year-old underground loader operator at a zinc and lead mine, living with his partner Ana with about three months of savings. He's union-minded and practical, open to new machines once they're proven, and already eyeing the tele-remote loader trial on level 9. He's calm in the plateau and uneasy under steady change, where his thoughts go straight to crewmates with more to lose. AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and reduced to saving and campaigning, but five or ten years lets him plan a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship. He admits that robots taking the deep levels would make the mine safer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is too short to finish a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies give real notice and pay into a training fund before automating, with wages paid while workers retrain.
